newsitem.title: DUBAI: Palestinian envoy meet Saudi officials on aid.
newsitem.headline: Palestinian envoy meet Saudi officials on aid.

text.p: A Palestinian envoy met Saudi cabinet ministers on Tuesday to seek funds for the cash-strapped Palestinian Authority, the Saudi official News Agency (SPA) reported.
Nabil Shaath, a close aide to Palestinian President Yasser Arafat, had talks with Foreign Minister Prince Saud al-Faisal and Finance and National Economy Minister Ibrahim al-Asaf.
Shaath is in charge of the Planning and International Cooperation portfolio in the Palestinian Authority, which runs the Gaza Strip and parts of the West Bank since 1994.

Palestinian sources said Shaath was seeking Saudi help to speed up the allocation of $60 million from pledged funds to build projects in Arab East Jerusalem designed to help preserve the divided city's Moslem heritage, buildings and shrines.
This gained urgency after Israel's move last September to open a tunnel beside the al-Aqsa Mosque in East Jerusalem, which Israel captured in 1967 Arab-Israeli war.

Saudi Arabia has already paid $73 million and given another $37 million to current development projects out of $200 million it pledged to the Palestinian Authority in 1994 and 1995, the Palestinian sources added.
SPA gave no details on the meetings. It said Shaath was accompanied by Rolf Anderson, special Middle East coordinator for Norway's Foreign Minister Bjoern Tore Godal.
Norway chairs an ad-hoc liaison committee of countries donating to Palestinian finances in which Saudi is a key donor.

Godal said after talks with Arafat last week that donor countries had pledged almost enough aid to plug the Palestinian Authority's deficit and it would continue to press them to honour their aid promises.
Diplomats said international donors would hold a November 19-21 meeting in Paris.
The self-rule Palestinian areas face financial crisis since Israel closed its borders with the West Bank and Gaza after a wave of suicide bombings in February and March.

Israeli officials have sometimes eased restrictions against Palestinian workers, only to reinforce them when violence flared up again. Palestinians say the closure is costing their economy between $7 million to $9 million per day.
